title: Lewis and Clark Expedition
summary: On 14 May 1804 William Clark and the Corps of Discovery left Camp River Dubois near St. Louis. They wintered at Fort Mandan among the Mandan and Hidatsa, reached the Pacific coast by November 1805, built Fort Clatsop for the winter, and returned to St. Louis on 23 September 1806. Native nations supplied information, horses and hospitality along the way.

reviewer_note: Native roles come from NPS and a non-tribal heritage foundation; no tribal-nation source was opened (Shoshone-Bannock, Mandan Hidatsa Arikara Nation, Nez Perce and Clatsop pages still to add). Sacagawea is described as Shoshone; the foundation page says she was an interpreter, not a guide. Camp River Dubois is placed at the St. Louis point with 40 km uncertainty because no opened page gives its coordinates. Waypoint years are day-of-year fractions: 1804.37 = 14 May; 1804.82 = 27 Oct; 1805.95 = mid December; 1806.73 = 23 Sept. Pacific arrival: NPS says by November 1805; the Washington University timeline says Clark's Ocian in view entry of 7 November was still about 20 miles from the sea.

beats.caption: Clark and the Corps of Discovery leave Camp River Dubois near St. Louis on 14 May 1804.
Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, interprets at the meeting with her brother Cameahwait's band, who sell horses to the expedition.
Back in St. Louis in September 1806, the party is credited with an impressive record of peaceful cooperation with the tribes it met.
